questions.stem: Which list gives the levels of biological classification in order, from the broadest to the most specific?
options: Kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species
Kingdom, class, phylum, family, order, species, genus
Phylum, kingdom, order, class, genus, family, species
Species, genus, family, order, class, phylum, kingdom
questions.explanation: Classification is hierarchical: each kingdom contains phyla, each phylum contains classes, and so on down to species. The last option is the right sequence but runs from most specific to broadest.

questions.stem: As you move from kingdom down to species in the classification hierarchy, what happens to the organisms in each group?
options: There are more of them, and they share fewer features
There are fewer of them, and they share more features
There are more of them, and they share more features
There are fewer of them, and they share fewer features
questions.explanation: A kingdom holds a huge range of organisms with only a few features in common. Each lower level holds fewer organisms that are more alike, until a species contains only one kind of organism.

questions.stem: The Tasmanian devil's scientific name is Sarcophilus harrisii. What does Sarcophilus name?
options: Its genus
Its species epithet
Its family
Its order
questions.explanation: In the binomial system, the first name is the genus (capitalised) and the second is the species epithet (lower case). Together they name the species.

questions.stem: Why do biologists use scientific names rather than common names?
options: Scientific names describe exactly where each species can be found
Scientific names change for each country so that locals can understand them
Common names cannot be used for any animal or plant that lives in Australia
Each species has one internationally recognised name, avoiding confusion
questions.explanation: Common names vary between places and languages and can refer to different species, but each species has one agreed scientific name, used worldwide. This is an international convention that aids communication.

questions.stem: Two animals are in the same family but different genera. Which other levels must they share?
options: Kingdom, phylum, class and order
Genus and species, but no others
Order and genus, but no others
Species, class, phylum and kingdom
questions.explanation: Because classification is hierarchical, organisms in the same family are also in the same order, class, phylum and kingdom. Being in different genera, they cannot share a species.

questions.stem: Mammals are divided into three groups: monotremes such as the platypus, marsupials such as the koala, and placental mammals such as humans. Which feature is used to separate them?
options: The number of chambers found in their hearts and lungs
Their method of reproduction and development of young
Whether or not they have hair or fur on their bodies
Whether or not they produce milk for their young
questions.explanation: Monotremes lay eggs, marsupials give birth to tiny young that usually develop in a pouch, and placental mammals nourish the young through a placenta before birth. All three groups have hair, produce milk and have four-chambered hearts.

questions.stem: Which feature is used to place a plant among the flowering plants rather than the conifers?
options: It has xylem and phloem to transport water and sugars
Its seeds develop inside a fruit formed from a flower
It reproduces sexually using male and female gametes
It contains chloroplasts and carries out photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Flowering plants produce seeds enclosed in fruits that develop from flowers, while conifers carry seeds in cones. Both reproduce sexually, photosynthesise and have xylem and phloem.

questions.stem: Two fungi look almost identical under the microscope, but their DNA sequences differ greatly. One is genetically very close to a fungus that looks quite different. How should they be classified?
options: In separate kingdoms, because they differ in their DNA sequences
By their DNA sequences, which better reflect their evolutionary relationships
By their appearance, because physical features are always the more reliable guide
In the same species, because they look almost identical to each other
questions.explanation: Molecular sequences reveal how recently organisms shared a common ancestor, so they are used to correct classifications when similar appearance has arisen independently. A DNA difference within fungi does not put them in different kingdoms.

questions.stem: What led biologists to group all living things into three domains: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya?
options: Microscopes showed that only some living things are made of cells
Fossils showed that animals appeared before any other living things
Dissections showed that fungi have the same organs as plants
Comparisons of molecular sequences showed two very different groups of prokaryotes
questions.explanation: Comparing molecular sequences, such as ribosomal RNA, showed that archaea differ from bacteria as much as either differs from eukaryotes, although both are prokaryotes. This led to the three-domain system.

questions.stem: Species A and B are in the same genus. Species C is in the same family but a different genus. What can be concluded about their relationships?
options: A and C are probably the most closely related, as they share a family
A and B are probably more closely related to each other than either is to C
C is probably more closely related to A than B is, as it is in the same family
All three are equally related, because they are all in the same family
questions.explanation: Modern classification aims to reflect evolutionary relatedness, so sharing a lower level such as genus usually indicates a more recent common ancestor. A and B share every level that C does, plus the genus.

questions.stem: A key reads: 1a. Legs present: go to 2. 1b. No legs: earthworm. 2a. Six legs: insect. 2b. Eight legs: spider. What is an animal with eight legs?
options: It cannot be keyed out
A spider
An insect
An earthworm
questions.explanation: The animal has legs, so step 1 leads to step 2, and eight legs leads to spider. Each step of a dichotomous key offers two contrasting choices.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a dichotomous key?
options: To identify an organism using a series of paired choices about its features
To show the evolutionary history of a group of species over time
To list every species found in an ecosystem by its abundance
To show the flow of energy between organisms in a food chain
questions.explanation: A dichotomous key leads the user through pairs of contrasting statements about observable features until the organism is identified. Evolutionary history is shown on a phylogenetic tree.

questions.stem: What kind of organisms were the earliest living things in the fossil record?
options: Simple land animals
Single-celled yeasts and fungi
Single-celled prokaryotes
Multicellular seaweeds
questions.explanation: The oldest fossils are of single-celled prokaryotes, including the microbes that built stromatolites. Eukaryotes, multicellular life and land organisms appeared much later.

questions.stem: Which order shows the first appearance of these groups in Earth's history, from earliest to most recent?
options: Multicellular organisms, animals on land, mammals, flowering plants
Mammals, multicellular organisms, flowering plants, animals on land
Animals on land, multicellular organisms, flowering plants, mammals
Flowering plants, mammals, animals on land, multicellular organisms
questions.explanation: Multicellular life appeared in the sea long before any animals moved onto land. Mammals arose around the time of the early dinosaurs, and flowering plants appeared later, during the age of the dinosaurs.

questions.stem: Which change had to occur before animals could live permanently on land?
options: Mammals evolved, providing prey for land predators
The dinosaurs became extinct, leaving empty habitats
Plants colonised the land, providing food and shelter
Flowering plants evolved, providing nectar for insects
questions.explanation: Land animals need food on land, and plants colonised the land first, forming the base of land food chains. Flowering plants, mammals and the extinction of the dinosaurs all came long after animals were on land.

questions.stem: Fossils of the earliest flowering plants are found in rocks that also contain dinosaur fossils, but no flowering plant fossils are found in much older rocks containing the first mammals. What does this show?
options: Flowering plants were present before the first mammals but did not form fossils
Flowering plants appeared after the first mammals, while dinosaurs still lived
Flowering plants appeared before the first mammals, and caused their evolution
Mammals and flowering plants appeared at the same time, before the dinosaurs
questions.explanation: The order of appearance in rock layers shows the order of first appearance in time. With no flowering plants in the older mammal-bearing rocks, the best supported conclusion is that they appeared later.

questions.stem: What is divergent evolution?
options: A species staying the same over millions of years without change
Two species evolving together, each adapting to changes in the other
Related species evolving different features from a common ancestor
Unrelated species evolving similar features in similar environments
questions.explanation: In divergent evolution, populations descended from one ancestor become adapted to different ways of life and come to differ. Unrelated species becoming similar is convergent evolution.

questions.stem: Australian marsupials include kangaroos, koalas, wombats and possums, which are adapted to very different ways of life but share a common ancestor. What does this show?
options: Divergent evolution from a common ancestor
Convergent evolution of unrelated groups
Mass extinction of ancestral marsupials
Asexual reproduction producing much variation
questions.explanation: One ancestral marsupial group diversified into many forms suited to different habitats and diets, an example of divergent evolution (adaptive radiation). Convergent evolution involves unrelated groups becoming similar.

questions.stem: The thylacine (Tasmanian tiger), a marsupial, had a skull very like that of a wolf, a placental mammal. How is this best explained?
options: Gene flow: wolves and thylacines interbred, sharing alleles for skull shape
Classification error: the thylacine was really a wolf that had a pouch
Convergent evolution: similar ways of life selected similar features in unrelated groups
Divergent evolution: the thylacine and wolf evolved from a recent common ancestor
questions.explanation: The thylacine and wolf are only distantly related, but both were predators of other animals, so similar selection pressures produced similar skulls: convergent evolution. Their ways of reproducing show they are in different groups of mammals.

questions.stem: A sugar glider (a marsupial) and a North American flying squirrel (a placental mammal) both have a skin membrane between their limbs for gliding. Which type of structure is the gliding membrane?
options: A homologous structure, resulting from convergent evolution
An analogous structure, resulting from convergent evolution
A homologous structure, resulting from divergent evolution
A vestigial structure, inherited from a gliding ancestor
questions.explanation: The two animals belong to different mammal groups and evolved gliding membranes independently in response to similar ways of life, so the membranes are analogous. Homologous structures are inherited from a common ancestor.

questions.stem: What is a mass extinction?
options: A geologically short period in which a large proportion of species die out
The gradual loss of one species after a long period of decline
The death of many individuals of one species in a single bad season
The replacement of one species by its descendants through evolution
questions.explanation: A mass extinction is a relatively sudden loss of a large proportion of Earth's species across many groups. The fossil record shows five major mass extinctions.

questions.stem: About 66 million years ago, a mass extinction wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs. What happened to the mammals afterwards?
options: They stopped evolving, because there were no longer any large predators
They evolved into birds, which replaced the dinosaurs on land
They diversified into many new forms, filling the roles the dinosaurs had left
They became extinct soon after, because they relied on dinosaurs for food
questions.explanation: After the extinction, surviving mammals radiated into many niches that had been occupied by dinosaurs, a pattern of divergent evolution following a mass extinction. Birds are descended from dinosaurs, not mammals.

questions.stem: Which pattern does the fossil record show after each mass extinction?
options: The same species that died out reappear quickly once the conditions improve
Life stays at low diversity permanently, so the diversity never recovers
Only single-celled organisms survive, and multicellular life evolves again
Surviving groups diversify over millions of years, producing many new species
questions.explanation: Extinct species do not reappear. Instead, survivors diversify into the habitats and roles left empty, so diversity recovers over millions of years, but with different groups dominant.

questions.stem: The earliest mammals were small and lived alongside dinosaurs for over 100 million years. Large and diverse mammals appear only in rocks younger than the extinction of the non-avian dinosaurs. Which explanation is best supported?
options: The extinction caused mutations in mammals that made them all grow larger
The extinction removed competitors and predators, opening roles that mammals evolved to fill
Mammals caused the extinction of the dinosaurs by eating their eggs in great numbers
Mammals did not exist before the extinction, so they evolved directly from dinosaurs
questions.explanation: The timing suggests that the loss of dinosaurs freed up resources and habitats, allowing mammals to diversify. The fossil record shows mammals existed long before the extinction, and mutations are not caused to order.
